questions.q:
Text C – The Night Ferry (paragraph 2)

(2) The harbour was a black mouth, and the ferry slid into it with its lights blazing like a lantern carried into a cave. Ropes groaned against the bollards. Gulls, startled from their sleep, wheeled overhead, shrieking accusations at the intruder. On the quay a single dock worker waited, hunched in his yellow coat, a lonely flame against the dark.

Identify the simile the writer uses to describe the ferry’s lights. [1]
ms: “like a lantern carried into a cave” (1) — allow “blazing like a lantern”
questions.model: “like a lantern carried into a cave”
questions.tip: A simile uses ‘like’ or ‘as’; a metaphor says something IS something else.

questions.q:
Text C – The Night Ferry (paragraph 2)

“Gulls, startled from their sleep, wheeled overhead, shrieking accusations at the intruder.”

(a) Identify the word that shows how the writer presents the ferry from the gulls’ point of view. [1]
(b) Explain what “shrieking accusations” suggests. [1]
ms: (a) “intruder” (1)
(b) The gulls’ loud cries sound angry, as if they are blaming/complaining about the ferry for disturbing them (1)
questions.model:
(a) “intruder”
(b) The gulls’ harsh cries sound like angry people blaming the ferry for waking them, as though it has no right to be there.
questions.tip: Personification often reveals a point of view — here, the ferry is an unwelcome visitor.

questions.q:
Text C – The Night Ferry (paragraph 2)

“The harbour was a black mouth, and the ferry slid into it …”

Explain the meaning and the effect of “The harbour was a black mouth”. [3]
ms: Meaning: the harbour entrance is dark and open/wide (1)
Effect: metaphor makes the harbour seem like a creature about to swallow the ferry (1)
Effect: creates menace/danger, a sense of being consumed or trapped; ‘black’ suggests the unknown/fear (1)
Allow: contrasts with the lit ferry, which looks small and vulnerable entering it (1)
questions.model: The harbour entrance is a dark, open space in the night. The metaphor turns it into the mouth of a huge creature, so as the ferry “slid into it” it seems to be swallowed. “Black” adds a sense of the unknown, making the arrival feel menacing and making the brightly lit ferry seem small and vulnerable.
questions.tip: Follow an image through the sentence: ‘mouth’ + ‘slid into it’ = being swallowed.

questions.q:
A student wrote this comment on a phrase from paragraph 4 of The Night Ferry:

“‘The engines purred beneath the floor like a vast contented cat’ is a simile. It makes it vivid and helps the reader imagine it.”

Rewrite the comment so that it explains the meaning and the effect of the phrase precisely. [4]
ms: Meaning: the engines make a low, steady, continuous hum/vibration under the floor (1)
Effect of ‘purred’/‘contented’: suggests comfort, safety, relaxation — the ship feels calm and cosy (1)
Effect of ‘vast’: a huge, powerful force that is nevertheless tame/gentle (1)
Link: fits the warm, sleepy atmosphere below deck / contrasts with the threatening harbour in paragraph 2 (1)
questions.model: The phrase means the engines give off a low, steady hum that can be felt through the floor. “Purred” and “contented” suggest a happy, relaxed cat, so the sound becomes comforting – the passengers feel safe and sleepy. “Vast” reminds us that the engines are huge and powerful, but here that power seems tame and gentle. This adds to the warm, cosy atmosphere below deck, in contrast with the dark, threatening harbour outside.
questions.tip: Ban the words ‘vivid’ and ‘helps the reader imagine’ — say WHAT the reader imagines and feels. Marking: No credit for ‘makes it vivid’ or naming the simile alone.

questions.q:
Text C – The Night Ferry

(2) “On the quay a single dock worker waited, hunched in his yellow coat, a lonely flame against the dark.”
(4) “An old man played cards with himself, slapping each one down as though it had personally insulted him.”

Explain the meaning and the effect of each of these descriptions of people, and comment on what they add to the passage. [5]
ms: Dock worker — meaning: one man, bent over against the cold, in a bright coat (1)
Dock worker — effect: ‘lonely flame’ makes him a small point of light/warmth/life in a vast darkness; suggests isolation and vulnerability (1)
Old man — meaning: plays solitaire, putting cards down forcefully (1)
Old man — effect: humorous personification of the cards; suggests frustration, boredom or a grumpy character; adds lightness/human detail (1)
Comment: both are solitary figures; the first adds to the loneliness/menace outside, the second to the homely, slightly comic world inside — reinforcing the contrast between paragraphs (1)
questions.model:
The dock worker is alone, bent against the cold, in a yellow coat. Calling him “a lonely flame against the dark” makes his coat a tiny point of colour and warmth in the huge darkness; “lonely” emphasises how isolated and fragile he seems.
The old man is playing cards by himself and putting them down hard. The idea that each card had “personally insulted him” is comic – he seems grumpy, bored or competitive even against himself.
Both are solitary figures, but they create different moods: the dock worker adds to the cold, lonely atmosphere outside, while the old man adds a humorous, homely touch to the warm world below deck, strengthening the contrast between the two paragraphs.
questions.tip: Characters in descriptive passages usually reinforce the atmosphere — say how.

questions.q:
Allow about 25 minutes.

Text C – The Night Ferry

(2) The harbour was a black mouth, and the ferry slid into it with its lights blazing like a lantern carried into a cave. Ropes groaned against the bollards. Gulls, startled from their sleep, wheeled overhead, shrieking accusations at the intruder. On the quay a single dock worker waited, hunched in his yellow coat, a lonely flame against the dark.
(4) Below deck, the passenger lounge was a different country. Children slept in tangled heaps on the benches, their mothers’ coats thrown over them like tents. The air was thick and warm, smelling of coffee and damp wool, and the engines purred beneath the floor like a vast contented cat. An old man played cards with himself, slapping each one down as though it had personally insulted him.

Re-read paragraphs 2 and 4.
Explain how the writer uses language to convey meaning and to create effect in these paragraphs. Choose three examples of words or phrases from each paragraph to support your answer. Your choices should include the use of imagery. [15]
ms: Indicative content (other well-explained choices are credited):
P2 “a black mouth” — dark harbour entrance; metaphor of a creature swallowing the ferry; menace
P2 “slid” — smooth, quiet, almost secretive movement; ferry enters cautiously, slightly sinister
P2 “blazing like a lantern carried into a cave” — bright lights; small, brave source of light entering a vast unknown darkness; exploration/danger
P2 “Ropes groaned” — creaking under strain; personification of effort/pain; tension
P2 “shrieking accusations at the intruder” — angry cries; ferry is unwelcome, nature hostile
P2 “a lonely flame against the dark” — isolated worker; fragile warmth/life in surrounding darkness
P2 overall: dark, hostile, lonely night world; the ferry is an intruder
P4 “a different country” — completely different atmosphere; metaphor of crossing a border into another world
P4 “tangled heaps” — children sleeping in untidy piles; relaxed, trusting, exhausted; comic warmth
P4 “like tents” — coats as shelters; children camping safely; protection and adventure
P4 “thick and warm … coffee and damp wool” — stuffy but comforting; sensory, homely
P4 “purred … like a vast contented cat” — steady hum; huge power made gentle; safety and comfort
P4 “as though it had personally insulted him” — humorous personification; grumpy old man; lightness
P4 overall: warm, safe, sleepy, homely refuge — contrasts sharply with paragraph 2

levels.d: Wide-ranging discussion of carefully chosen language; explanations of meaning are precise and effects are analysed in detail at word level; imagery explored convincingly; clear understanding of how choices combine to create the overall impression and the contrast between paragraphs.
Appropriate choices with clear meanings; effects explained with some precision; imagery explained; some sense of overall impression.
Sensible choices; meanings mostly explained; effects identified but often general; some imagery attempted.
Some relevant choices but explanations are partial or mainly meanings; effects vague; may rely on naming techniques.
Few relevant choices; long quotations or repetition of the text; little explanation.

questions.model:
In paragraph 2 the night harbour is presented as hostile. “The harbour was a black mouth” turns the dark entrance into the jaws of a huge creature, and the ferry “slid” into it quietly, almost secretly, as if creeping into danger. The ferry’s lights are “blazing like a lantern carried into a cave”: “blazing” shows how bright they are, but the image of a lantern in a cave makes that light seem small and brave against a vast, unknown darkness. Even nature objects: the gulls are “shrieking accusations at the intruder”, so their cries become angry complaints and the ferry is clearly unwelcome. The single dock worker is “a lonely flame against the dark”, a tiny point of warmth in all this blackness, emphasising isolation. Overall, paragraph 2 creates a cold, threatening world in which light and people seem fragile.
Paragraph 4 is the complete opposite – literally “a different country”, as if passing below deck means crossing a border into a warmer world. The children sleep in “tangled heaps”, a phrase that suggests exhaustion but also total trust and relaxation; their mothers’ coats are thrown over them “like tents”, so they seem to be camping in safe little shelters. The engines “purred … like a vast contented cat”: the steady hum becomes a comforting sound, and “vast” reminds us of the engines’ huge power, now tame and gentle. Finally, the old man slaps down his cards “as though it had personally insulted him”, a comic touch that adds warmth and humanity.
Together the two paragraphs contrast danger and comfort: outside, darkness swallows and accuses; inside, everything is warm, protected and quietly funny.
questions.tip: Three choices per paragraph, each with meaning + word-level effect, then a sentence on overall impression — and mention the contrast.
